content: The protein p21, also referred to as p21Cip1 or p21Waf1, is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor (CKI) that can inhibit all cyclin/CDK complexes, although it is most commonly associated with the inhibition of CDK2. It is a critical downstream target of p53 activity and plays a pivotal role in linking DNA damage to cell cycle arrest. Function CDK Inhibition p21 is a potent cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor. The p21 (Cip1/Waf1) protein binds to and inhibits the activity of cyclin-CDK2, CDK1, and CDK4/6 complexes, thereby regulating cell cycle progression at the G1 and S phases. This binding occurs through the N-terminal domain of p21, which shares homology with other CIP/KIP family members, such as p27 and p57. Specifically, p21 contains a Cy1 motif in its N-terminal half and a weaker Cy2 motif in its C-terminal domain. These motifs allow p21 to bind CDKs in a manner that blocks their interaction with cyclins, thereby preventing CDK activation. Single-cell studies of CDK2 activity have demonstrated that p21 is responsible for a bifurcation in CDK2 activity following mitosis. Cells with high p21 levels enter a G0/quiescent state, while those with low p21 levels continue to proliferate. Further research has shown that this bistability is driven by a double-negative feedback loop between p21 and CDK2, where CDK2 inhibits p21 activity via ubiquitin ligase-mediated degradation. PCNA Inhibition p21 interacts with proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), a DNA polymerase accessory factor, and regulates DNA replication during the S phase and DNA damage repair. p21 has a high affinity for the PIP-box binding region on PCNA. Binding of p21 to this region is thought to block the binding of processivity factors required for PCNA-dependent S-phase DNA synthesis, while still allowing PCNA-dependent nucleotide excision repair (NER). As a result, p21 acts as an effective inhibitor of S-phase DNA synthesis but permits DNA repair, suggesting that p21 selectively modulates polymerase processivity factors depending on the context of DNA synthesis. Apoptosis Inhibition p21 can be cleaved by caspase-3-like proteases, leading to a dramatic activation of CDK2, which may play a role in the execution of apoptosis following caspase activation. However, p21 itself can inhibit apoptosis and does not independently induce cell death. It has also been reported to inhibit apoptosis in response to replication fork stress. Regulation p53-Dependent Response p21 is the primary mediator of p53-dependent cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage. Studies have shown that p21 is expressed in cells with wild-type p53 but not in those with mutant p53. Constitutive expression of p21 leads to cell cycle arrest in various cell types. For example, γ-irradiation of fibroblasts induces a p53and p21-dependent cell cycle arrest, with p21 found bound to inactive cyclin E/CDK2 complexes. Mouse models have demonstrated that while p21-deficient mice are healthy, they develop spontaneous tumors, and cells derived from these mice exhibit compromised G1 checkpoint control. Collectively, these findings establish p21 as the primary mediator of p53-dependent cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage. Recent single-cell studies have shown that pulsatile p53 activity leads to corresponding pulses of p21 activation. The strength of p21 activation is dependent on the cell cycle phase, highlighting the dynamic regulation of p21 in response to DNA damage. Degradation p21 is negatively regulated by ubiquitin ligases throughout the cell cycle and in response to DNA damage. During the G1/S transition, the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex SCFSkp2 induces p21 degradation. Additionally, the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex CRL4Cdt2 degrades p21 in a PCNA-dependent manner during the S phase, which is necessary to prevent p21-dependent re-replication. CRL4Cdt2 also mediates p21 degradation in response to UV irradiation. Recent studies in human cell lines have shown that SCFSkp2 degrades p21 toward the end of the G1 phase, allowing cells to exit a quiescent state. In contrast, CRL4Cdt2 degrades p21 at a much higher rate during the G1/S transition and maintains low p21 levels throughout the S phase. Clinical Significance Cytoplasmic expression of p21 is significantly correlated with lymph node metastasis, distant metastases, advanced TNM stage (tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis), depth of invasion, and overall survival (OS) rates. In malignant thymic epithelial tumors, p21 expression negatively influences survival and is significantly associated with WHO type B2/B3 classifications. When combined with low p27 and high p53 expression, disease-free survival (DFS) decreases. p21 mediates resistance of hematopoietic cells to HIV infection by forming a complex with HIV integrase, thereby preventing chromosomal integration of the provirus. HIV-infected individuals who naturally suppress viral replication exhibit elevated levels of p21 and its associated mRNA. p21 expression affects at least two stages of the HIV life cycle in CD4 T cells, significantly limiting the production of new viruses. In metastatic canine mammary tumors, increased p21 levels are observed in both primary tumors and their metastases, despite increased cell proliferation. Interestingly, mice lacking the p21 gene gain the ability to regenerate lost appendages. Interactions p21 has been shown to interact with the following proteins: Nrf2 BCCIP CIZ1 CUL4A CCNE1 CDK DDB1 DTL GADD45A GADD45G HDAC PCNA PIM1 TK1 TSG101
